links.outcome: Standalone AI vs first-reader radiologists on cancer detection accuracy, same data
links.effect: AI matched at first-reader specificity was comparable on all measures (sensitivity 62.6% vs 63.5%, p=0.43); AI matched at sensitivity had lower specificity (97.5% vs 97.7%) and higher recall rate; different cancers detected.
links.quote: Standalone AI spec did not differ statistically significantly from the first reader across any accuracy measures (Table 2 ).

links.outcome: Validation on leakage-free, consecutive, population-representative mammograms not used in AI training
links.effect: Validated on 249,402 consecutive screenings from an entire regional population; images never used for AI training/validation/testing.
links.quote: The mammograms in this study have never been used for training, validation, or testing of the AI system.

links.outcome: Effect of AI decision threshold choice on accuracy relative to readers
links.effect: Threshold matched at reader specificity gave equivalent accuracy; threshold matched at sensitivity gave lower specificity (97.5% vs 97.7%), PPV 17.5% vs 18.7%, and higher recall rate (3.0% vs 2.8%).
links.quote: The accuracy of the AI system was comparable to that of first readers in a double-read mammography screening population, mainly when the AI score cut-off was matched at first reader specificity, highlighting the importance of choosing an appropriate threshold.

links.outcome: Generalizability of AI performance to a different population/setting
links.effect: Single mammography vendor, single region; authors note accuracy estimates could differ in populations with different prevalence or characteristics; thresholds derived from the study dataset.
links.quote: Although our findings might transfer to similar populations, accuracy estimates could differ in populations with a different breast cancer prevalence or significantly different population characteristics.

links.outcome: Accuracy and recall at AI thresholds
links.effect: AI_sens: specificity 97.5% vs 97.7%, PPV 17.5% vs 18.7%, RR 3.0% vs 2.8%, all worse than first readers.
links.quote: AI<sub>sens</sub> had lower specificity (97.5% vs 97.7%; p < 0.0001) and PPV (17.5% vs 18.7%; p = 0.01) and a higher RR (3.0% vs 2.8%; p < 0.0001) than first readers.

links.effect: AI_spec sensitivity 62.6% vs 63.5% (p=0.43), specificity 97.7% vs 97.7% (p=0.96); PPV/NPV/RR also nonsignificant.
links.quote: Standalone AI spec did not differ statistically significantly from the first reader across any accuracy measures (Table 2 ).

links.effect: AI_sens/AI_spec detected fewer screen-detected cancers (1166/1156 vs 1252) but more interval cancers (126/117 vs 39), p<0.0001.
links.quote: Both AI<sub>sens</sub> and AI<sub>spec</sub> detected significantly fewer screen-detected cancers (1166 (AI<sub>sens</sub>), 1156 (AI<sub>spec</sub>) vs 1252; p < 0.0001) but found more interval cancers compared to first readers (126 (AI<sub>sens</sub>), 117 (AI<sub>spec</sub>) vs 39; p < 0.0001) with varying types of cancers detected across multiple subgroups.

links.outcome: cancer detection discrepancy between standalone AI and first readers
links.effect: Standalone AI at both thresholds disagreed with first readers in 23% of cancer cases, being either detected by AI and missed by first reader or vice versa
links.quote: Moreover, subgroup analyses of detection agreements and discrepancies between the AI and first reader showed that Standalone AI at both thresholds disagreed with the first reader in 23% of all cancer cases, which were either detected by AI and missed by the first reader or vice versa (Supplementary eTable 4 ).
